passage:
Day 1. On the first smoggy morning at the university library, everyone wore masks. Hrithik told a joke to his friend Pankaj at the desk and saw only his eyes above the cloth. No smile, no laugh. He decided the joke had flopped.
Day 3. He noticed Pankaj's eyes crinkling at the corners whenever something was funny, and his voice lifting. Hrithik realised he'd been looking for a mouth that was hidden.
Day 6. He asked, "Did that last joke land? I can't see your face." Pankaj laughed, muffled. "I've been grinning behind here all week!"

qa.q: Where were Hrithik and Pankaj on the first smoggy morning?
qa.a: They were at the university library.

qa.q: What did Hrithik feel when he saw only Pankaj's eyes and heard no laugh?
qa.a: Hrithik probably felt disappointed, sure his joke had flopped, though he was missing the smile hidden by the mask.

qa.q: What did Hrithik learn to use instead of a visible smile?
qa.a: He learned to watch Pankaj's eyes and voice, and to ask directly when he couldn't tell.

qa.q: How might Pankaj have felt when Hrithik asked whether the joke landed?
qa.a: He was probably amused and pleased that Hrithik cared, and a bit surprised that his grin had been invisible.

grounding: A person in a mask shows only eyes and upper face, so voice, eyes and asking directly carry more weight.

passage: "Back in my workshop days, Harsha, dust was so thick that we tied cloths over our noses and mouths," said Uday, tapping his granddaughter's mask. "I couldn't tell whether a customer was pleased or vexed. I used to stand there guessing." He smiled behind his cup. "Then I began to watch the eyes and listen. A pleased customer's voice went warm and quick. A doubtful one spoke slowly. If I couldn't tell, I said, 'Are you happy with the work?' They always told me." Harsha frowned. "Isn't asking rude?" "Never. Better to ask than to imagine. Half the time I'd have been wrong about the faces I couldn't see."

qa.q: What did Uday and the workshop workers tie over their noses and mouths?
qa.a: They tied cloths over their noses and mouths.

qa.q: What was Uday feeling when he couldn't see his customers' faces?
qa.a: He felt unsure and stuck guessing whether they were pleased or vexed, until he found other cues.

qa.q: What could Harsha do when she can't read someone in a mask?
qa.a: She could listen for warmth in the voice, watch the eyes, and ask kindly if she is not sure.

qa.q: How might the customers have felt when Uday asked whether they were happy?
qa.a: They probably felt respected and glad to be heard, since they always told him.

grounding: A person in a mask shows only eyes and upper face, so voice, eyes and words carry more weight and asking directly helps.

passage:
The college clinic in Guwahati was packed that morning, and Bidisha was volunteering at the registration desk for the health camp. Everyone wore masks. Babies cried, names were called over a crackling speaker, and the fan made the forms fly.
Her fellow volunteer, Anjali, kept looking at her with narrowed eyes. Bidisha couldn't see her mouth. Was she annoyed? Had Bidisha filled something wrong?
During a lull, Bidisha leaned over. "Anjali, are you upset with me? I can't tell with the masks."
Anjali's eyes widened, then crinkled. "No! I'm squinting because I left my glasses at home. And I've been smiling at you all morning. You couldn't see?"
"All I see is eyes."
"Then I'll use words. You're doing great."
After that, they said things out loud: "Good job." "Can you take this one?" "Thanks!" The desk ran smoother. And Bidisha started noticing Anjali's eyes crinkling above the mask when she was actually smiling.

qa.q: What had Anjali left at home?
qa.a: Her glasses.

qa.q: What was Bidisha feeling when Anjali kept narrowing her eyes?
qa.a: Bidisha felt anxious and unsure, worried Anjali was annoyed with her.

qa.q: What made the desk run smoother?
qa.a: Saying things out loud and asking directly, because masks hid smiles and left only eyes to read.

qa.q: What was it like for Anjali behind her mask?
qa.a: Anjali was friendly and smiling all morning, but squinting without her glasses, which the mask made look like annoyance.

grounding: The scene shows masks hiding smiles and lower-face signals, and words and a direct question replacing guesswork.

passage:
The smog in Delhi was so thick that November that everyone at the college wore masks. Tushar had joined the drama society, and his scene partner was Sudha.
At the first rehearsal, he tried a joke. Sudha's eyes stayed still above her mask. He couldn't see if she smiled. He tried another. Same.
By the third rehearsal, he was sure she disliked him. He stopped joking.
After practice, walking to the metro, Sudha said, "You've gone quiet. Did I do something?"
Tushar blinked. "I thought you hated my jokes. You never laughed."
Sudha pulled down her mask for a second. She was grinning. "I laugh every time! Silently. Under the mask. My laugh is embarrassing."
"I couldn't see anything."
"Then listen for this." She snorted. "That means funny."
Tushar laughed. "Okay. Snort means funny."
From then on, they talked more and guessed less.

qa.q: What did Sudha do after pulling down her mask?
qa.a: She was grinning.

qa.q: What was Tushar feeling by the third rehearsal?
qa.a: Tushar felt discouraged and insecure, sure Sudha disliked him because he couldn't see her react.

qa.q: What did the two of them do that fixed the misunderstanding?
qa.a: They asked each other directly and agreed on clearer signals, like words and Sudha's snort, since masks hid their faces.

qa.q: How did Sudha experience the rehearsals?
qa.a: Sudha was laughing silently under her mask the whole time and noticed Tushar going quiet, so she asked.

grounding: The scene shows masks hiding smiles, leading to a misreading, and words and direct questions carrying more weight.

passage:
"Rekha, are you upset about the results?"
Rekha looked up from the microscope. Above her lab mask, her eyes were steady. "No. Why?"
"You haven't said anything for ten minutes. And your eyes look serious."
"Parul, I'm smiling. I've been smiling at these cells since they turned blue. The experiment worked!"
Parul laughed. "I can't see your mouth! You could be crying under there."
"I'm not crying. I'm delighted. Can't you tell from my eyes?"
"Honestly? Your delighted eyes and your annoyed eyes look the same."
Rekha thought about it. "Fine. New rule. When we're masked, we say the feeling out loud."
"Okay. I'm relieved. And a bit jealous your sample worked first."
"I'm proud. And hungry."
"Say the feeling. Got it."
They both laughed, and this time Parul could hear it.

qa.q: What colour did the cells turn?
qa.a: The cells turned blue.

qa.q: What was Parul feeling when Rekha stayed silent?
qa.a: Parul felt worried and unsure, reading Rekha's serious eyes as upset about the results.

qa.q: What rule did they agree on, and why does it help?
qa.a: To say their feelings out loud when masked, because masks hide smiles and eyes alone can be misread.

qa.q: How did Rekha feel during those ten minutes?
qa.a: Rekha felt delighted and proud that the experiment worked, though the mask hid her smile.

grounding: The dialogue shows masks hiding smiles, and words carrying more weight than eyes alone.

passage: In my first month as a trainee at the dental clinic, everyone wore masks all day, and I realised how much I had been reading mouths my whole life. When I explained a bill to a man at the front desk, I couldn't tell if he was smiling politely or gritting his teeth. His eyes crinkled, but that could have been squinting at the screen. I kept over-explaining, just in case. Payal, the senior assistant, pulled me aside at lunch. "Bidisha, behind a mask your voice has to do what your smile used to. And their eyes and words are all you get, so listen to those. If you can't tell, ask." The next patient was a nervous girl with her mother. Her eyes were wide above the mask and her hands gripped the chair. I said warmly, "First time here? You can squeeze the armrest as hard as you like." She nodded. I asked, "Scared, or just cold? It's freezing in here." She laughed. "Both."

qa.q: What did Payal say the voice has to do behind a mask?
qa.a: The voice has to do what the smile used to.

qa.q: What was Bidisha feeling while explaining the bill?
qa.a: Bidisha felt unsure and a bit anxious, unable to tell whether the man was smiling or gritting his teeth, which led to over-explaining.

qa.q: What did Bidisha do differently with the next patient?
qa.a: Bidisha used a warm voice, read the girl's wide eyes and gripping hands, and asked directly whether she was scared or cold.

qa.q: What might the nervous girl have felt when asked 'Scared, or just cold?'
qa.a: The girl likely felt understood and a little lighter, laughing and admitting 'Both'.

grounding: It shows masks hiding smiles and lower-face signals, so a young adult relies on voice, eyes and words and asks directly.
